prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
The recent evolution of 3D content generation—shifting from optimization-based methods (like NeRF) to efficient feed-forward Gaussian Splatting—has enabled the synthesis of 3D assets in seconds. However, current steganography and watermarking techniques for 3D representations have not kept pace with this speed. Existing methods predominantly rely on per-scene training or optimization to embed information into a specific asset. This creates a severe bottleneck: while generating an object takes mere seconds, watermarking it can take minutes. This time overhead renders current protection mechanisms impractical for large-scale, real-time 3D asset deployment, creating a critical need for a watermarking framework that is as fast and scalable as the generation models themselves.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the watermarking pipeline can be unified with the 3D generation pipeline into a single, feed-forward process. By leveraging the semantic consistency of visual foundation models, we believe we can inject steganographic information directly into the intermediate features of a 3D generative model without requiring per-scene optimization.

Our intuition is that a generative network can learn to satisfy two objectives simultaneously: synthesizing high-fidelity 3D geometry/texture and encoding hidden signals within the Gaussian attributes, provided the gradients between these two tasks are appropriately harmonized during training. This would reduce the marginal time cost of watermarking to near zero.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a framework, "InstantSplamp," designed to integrate invisible information into 3D Gaussian Splatting generation. The approach consists of three conceptual modules:

**1. Semantic Feature Injection (Embedding Stage)**
Instead of directly embedding raw pixel data, we will utilize a pre-trained visual foundation model to extract robust semantic features from the target watermark (hidden information). Simultaneously, as the generative model processes the input image to create 3D Gaussians, we will intercept its intermediate feature maps. We propose using a cross-attention mechanism to inject the watermark features into these intermediate generative features. This allows the hidden signal to subtly influence the resulting 3D representation in a way that is semantically coherent rather than just adding pixel noise.

**2. View-Dependent Recovery (Decoding Stage)**
To recover the hidden information, we will define a specific "checking viewpoint." When the generated 3D Gaussians are rendered from this specific pose, the resulting 2D image should contain the retrievable watermark. We will employ a decoder network (e.g., a U-Net architecture) that takes this rendered view as input and reconstructs the original hidden data. We will enforce a contrastive objective: the decoder must recover the watermark from the watermarked render but should output a null result when processing a standard, non-watermarked render.

**3. Adaptive Gradient Harmonization (Optimization Strategy)**
A core challenge is that the objective of "perfect rendering quality" often conflicts with "robust information hiding." Naive loss combination often leads to one task dominating the other. To address this, we will implement an adaptive gradient harmonization strategy. During training, we will compute the gradients for both the visual reconstruction loss and the steganography loss. We will introduce a masking mechanism that filters gradient updates based on their alignment; specifically, we will update weights only when the directions of the two objectives are not in severe conflict (e.g., via cosine similarity analysis). This ensures the network finds a parameter space that satisfies both visual fidelity and decoding accuracy.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Zero-Overhead Watermarking:** We expect to eliminate the need for per-scene optimization, allowing 3D assets to be watermarked instantly during their generation phase.
*   **Scalability:** This approach will enable the practical protection of intellectual property in large-scale, automated 3D content creation pipelines.
*   **Theoretical Generalization:** We aim to demonstrate that feed-forward 3D generative models possess sufficient capacity to handle multimodal steganography (images, text, audio) without degrading the perceptual quality of the 3D output.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the InstantSplamp framework to assess its performance in 3D steganography, focusing on rendering quality, hidden information recovery, and computational efficiency.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Source:** A filtered subset of the Objaverse dataset.
    *   **Filtering Criteria:** Excluded low-quality 3D models (partial scans, objects without textures).
    *   **Total Size:** Approximately 80,000 3D objects.
    *   **Training Split:** 100 randomly selected objects.
    *   **Test Split:** 100 unseen objects reserved for evaluation.
    *   **Rendering Settings:** RGBA images rendered from 40 camera views at a resolution of 256 x 256 for both training and testing.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Rendering Quality:** Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS).
    *   **Hidden Information Recovery:** PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS.
    *   **Subjective Quality:** Human evaluation scores (averaged from 20 volunteers viewing 360-degree rotational videos of 30 randomly selected samples).
    *   **Multimodal Recovery Metrics:**
        *   Text: Accuracy (ACC).
        *   QR Codes: SSIM.
        *   Audio/Video: PSNR.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Init. Render:** The initial rendering without any watermarking (upper bound for rendering quality).
    *   **LSB (Least Significant Bit):** Traditional 2D steganography method.
    *   **DeepStega:** A deep learning-based 2D steganography pipeline.
    *   **StegaNeRF:** A NeRF-based steganography framework, redesigned/adapted for a Gaussian Splatting pipeline for fair comparison.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Gaussian Generator:** LGM (Large Multi-view Gaussian Model).
    *   **Hidden Decoder:** A simple U-Net architecture.
    *   **Optimization:** Fine-tuned a LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) for each watermark image.
    *   **Training Duration:** Approximately 30 epochs over 100 objects, taking roughly 20 minutes.
    *   **Optimizer:** AdamW with a learning rate of 1e-4.
    *   **Loss Weights:** $\lambda_1 = 0.3$ (decoder positive), $\lambda_2 = 1$ (decoder negative), $\lambda_3 = 0.1$ (RGB rendering).

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

## 3. Qualitative Observations

We derived the following observations from the visual data, comparative figures, and textual analysis:

**Efficiency and Overhead Observations:**
*   Traditional per-scene watermarking methods required approximately 6 minutes for watermarking on top of generation time (N * 6 min).
*   Our method (InstantSplamp) unified 3D generation and watermarking into a single process with a time cost of N * 12 seconds.
*   We observed that InstantSplamp reduced the watermarking overhead from approximately 30 times the generation time to nearly zero.

**Visual Fidelity and Recovery (Qualitative Comparisons):**
*   **DeepStega:** We observed visible artifacts in the recovered watermarks, indicating a struggle to maintain high fidelity in the hidden image.
*   **StegaNeRF:** We noted that while it recovered watermarks better than DeepStega, the rendering quality of the 3D object itself suffered (e.g., blurry textures) compared to the initial render.
*   **InstantSplamp:** We observed that our method retained the original rendering details (texture and geometry) while precisely recovering the watermark. The rendered images appeared visually identical to the unwatermarked baselines.
*   We confirmed this performance on unseen objects (e.g., cats, anime figures, birds), where InstantSplamp consistently preserved details and recovered watermarks where baselines failed or degraded quality.

**Multimodal Embedding Performance:**
We successfully embedded and recovered various data modalities. We recorded the following specific metrics for sample objects:
*   **Text Embedding ("Have a nice day!", etc.):**
    *   Recovery Accuracy: 100%.
    *   Recovery Accuracy: 100%.

*   **QR Code Embedding:**
    *   Sample 1 Recovery SSIM: 0.996.
    *   Sample 2 Recovery SSIM: 0.995.

*   **Audio Embedding:**
    *   Sample 1 Recovery PSNR: 49.65.

**Robustness Analysis:**
*   **JPEG Compression:** We observed that the hidden image recovery SSIM remained stable (between 0.90 and 0.95) even as the JPEG compression rate increased from 0.0 to 0.8. The rendering SSIM showed a slight decline but remained consistent.
*   **Gaussian Blur:** We observed a decrease in hidden image recovery SSIM as the Gaussian Blur standard deviation increased from 0.0 to 1.0, but the SSIM remained above 0.85, indicating resilience.
*   **Variability:** The shaded regions in our analysis (representing 0.5 standard deviation) indicated consistent performance across selected scenes despite data variability.

**Ablation Analysis Findings:**

*   Removing Adaptive Gradient Harmonization lowered both rendering and recovery scores compared to the full model, validating the strategy of aligning gradient updates.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex
\begin{figure}[h]
\begin{center}
%\framebox[4.0in]{$\;$}
\fbox{\rule[-.5cm]{0cm}{4cm} \rule[-.5cm]{4cm}{0cm}}
\end{center}
\caption{Sample figure caption.}
\end{figure}
```

### Example Code for Tables
```latex
\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Sample table title}
\label{sample-table}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---
### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.
- Attempt to recall or reconstruct any existing or published paper.
- Use external facts, assumptions, or prior familiarity with the work.
- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.
- Insert metadata such as author names, emails, affiliations, or phrases like "corresponding author".

#### Anonymity Requirement
The paper must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.  
Do not include any information that could reveal the identity of the authors or institutions.

#### Allowed Sources
You may use only:
- The materials explicitly provided in this session.
- Logical reasoning derived from those materials.

#### Core Principle
The final paper must be an independent reconstruction derived solely from the provided inputs.  
This constraint is strict and overrides all other instructions.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The recent evolution of 3D content generation has shifted from slow optimization-based methods (like SDS) to efficient feed-forward techniques capable of generating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assets in seconds. However, a critical bottleneck remains in the protection and watermarking of these assets. Existing steganographic methods for 3D representations (meshes, NeRF, or 3DGS) rely heavily on per-scene or per-object optimization. While asset generation takes mere seconds, the watermarking process often requires minutes of separate training time—creates a time overhead that is multiples of the generation time itself. This efficiency gap renders current watermarking techniques impractical for the large-scale deployment of generative 3D models. We face a need for a framework that can invisibly watermark generated 3D assets *during* the generation process itself, eliminating the need for post-generation optimization.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **InstantSplamp** (Instant Splatting Stamp), a framework designed to seamlessly integrate steganography into the feed-forward pass of large 3D generative models. Our central hypothesis is that we can utilize visual foundation models to extract semantic watermark embeddings and inject them into the intermediate feature space of a 3D Gaussian generator via cross-attention mechanisms.

By doing so, we aim to decouple the watermarking process from per-scene optimization. We predict that by aligning the gradients of the information-hiding objective with the rendering quality objective using a novel Adaptive Gradient Harmonization strategy, we can achieve high-fidelity watermark recovery from rendered views without compromising the visual quality of the generated 3D Gaussians.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will build our framework upon an image-to-3D generative model, $F_{\Theta}$, which converts an input image $I$ into a set of 3D Gaussians parameters $\pmb{\Omega} = F_{\Theta}(I)$. The parameters $\pmb{\Omega}$ include centers $\mathbf{x}$, scaling factors $\mathbf{s}$, rotations $\mathbf{q}$, opacity $\alpha$, and color features $\mathbf{c}$.

Our methodology involves two distinct stages: **Hidden Information Embedding** and **Hidden Information Recovery**, governed by a specialized optimization strategy.

### 1. Hidden Information Embedding
To embed a hidden signal (watermark) $H$, we will employ a hidden embedder $F_{\Phi}$. We observe that standard 2D-to-3D projection is ill-posed; therefore, simply adding a watermark to the input image is insufficient. Instead, we will leverage the **DINOv2** encoder to extract robust, semantically consistent spatial features, denoted as $f_H$, from the hidden information $H$.

We will inject these features directly into the intermediate feature maps $f_I$ of the generative backbone using a cross-attention mechanism. This allows the hidden information to influence the 3D representation construction adaptively. The update rule for the intermediate feature $f_I$ will be defined as:

$$ f_I := \mathrm{Softmax} \left( \frac { K \cdot Q ^ { T } } { \sqrt { d } } \right) \cdot V $$

where $d$ denotes the feature dimension. The Query ($Q$), Key ($K$), and Value ($V$) matrices are derived as follows:

$$ K = F_{\Phi_K}(f_H), \quad V = F_{\Phi_V}(f_H), \quad Q = F_{\Phi_Q}(f_I) $$

Here, $F_{\Phi_K}$ and $F_{\Phi_V}$ are linear transformation layers applied to the hidden features $f_H$, while $F_{\Phi_Q}$ is applied to the generator's intermediate features $f_I$.

### 2. Hidden Information Recovery
To recover the watermark, we will utilize a specific "checking viewpoint" pose, denoted as $P_C$. The decoder, $F_{\Psi}$ (implemented as a U-Net), will attempt to extract the hidden signal $H$ from the image rendered at this specific view, $\Omega(P_C)$.

To ensure robustness and prevent false positives, we will implement a contrastive loss mechanism. We define two decoding loss terms:
1.  **Positive Decoding Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{dec^+}$):** Ensures the decoder recovers $H$ from the watermarked rendering.
2.  **Negative Decoding Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{dec^-}$):** Ensures the decoder extracts a predefined null/constant image $\mathcal{O}$ when fed a rendering from a non-steganographic generator $\Omega_0(P_C)$.

$$ \mathcal{L}_{dec^+} = | F_{\Psi}(\Omega(P_C)) - H |, \quad \mathcal{L}_{dec^-} = | F_{\Psi}(\Omega_0(P_C)) - \mathcal{O} | $$

### 3. Optimization and Loss Formulation
We will optimize the generative model $\Theta$, embedder $\Phi$, and decoder $\Psi$ end-to-end. To maintain visual fidelity, we include a photometric loss $\mathcal{L}_{rgb} = | \Omega(P) - \Omega_0(P) |$ between the watermarked output and the original non-watermarked output across various poses $P$.

The total objective function will be:

$$ \mathcal{L}(I, H; \Theta, \Phi, \Psi) = \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{dec^+} + \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{dec^-} + \lambda_3 \mathcal{L}_{rgb} $$

where $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3$ are trade-off coefficients.

### 4. Adaptive Gradient Harmonization
A critical challenge we anticipate is the conflict between rendering quality and information hiding during the update of the generator weights $\Theta$. Naive optimization may degrade generation quality to satisfy the steganographic constraint.

To address this, we will implement **Adaptive Gradient Harmonization**. We will compute a gradient mask $\mathcal{M} \in \mathbb{R}^N$ for the weights $\Theta$. This mask effectively filters out gradient updates where the objective of rendering fidelity conflicts with the objective of watermark embedding. We define the mask using the cosine similarity of the gradients:

$$ \mathcal{M} = \mathbb{I} \left( \mathrm{Cos} \left( \frac { \partial \mathcal { L } _ { r g b } } { \partial \Theta } , \frac { \partial ( \mathcal { L } _ { d e c ^ { + } } + \mathcal { L } _ { d e c ^ { - } } ) } { \partial \Theta } \right) > 0 \right) $$

where $\mathbb{I}$ is the indicator function. During backpropagation, we will apply this mask to the global gradient update:

$$ \text{Update} \leftarrow \frac { \partial \mathcal { L } } { \partial \Theta } \odot \mathcal { M } $$

This ensures that we only update weights where the steganography and rendering objectives are aligned or orthogonal, preserving the pre-trained quality of the generative backbone.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Zero-Cost Watermarking:** We expect to demonstrate that high-fidelity steganography can be achieved with nearly zero additional time overhead compared to the base generation time, solving the scalability issue of per-scene optimization.
2.  **Feed-Forward Generalizability:** By training on a diverse dataset, we aim to produce a model capable of embedding watermarks into unseen objects without retraining.
3.  **Theoretical Alignment of Objectives:** The proposed Adaptive Gradient Harmonization will provide a theoretical basis for balancing the competing tasks of visual generation and information hiding within a single set of network weights.
4.  **Multimodal Capability:** While primarily designed for images, the architecture of the embedder and decoder will be constructed to support extending the hidden signal $H$ to other modalities (text, audio, video) by modifying the decoder branch to handle 1D vectors or sequence data.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
